ABSTRACT
PhotoVoltaic (PV) panels have been increasingly favored by residential users in recent years, due
to noticeable reductions in their costs. The PV systems become more effective when combined
with battery packages, which store the energy produced by the PV systems for later use. This way,
the PV systems are able to provide flexible and reliable services even when the peak demand for
electricity misalign with the window of most efficient PV power generation. In this study, we
develop an integrated charge/discharge scheme for lithium-ion batteries to maximize their total
expected benefit. Specifically, we develop a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model to maximize
the battery utilization, subject to uncertainty in weather conditions and electricity demands, while
accounting for battery degradation due to calendar aging and charging/discharging cycles. Due to
the extremely slow rate of degradation in batteries, the state space of the MDP is excessively
large. To solve the problem efficiently, we establish structural properties of the MDP and exploit
them to solve the problem. We improve the backward induction algorithm with established struc-
tural properties. We further improve the Deep Q-network (DQN) algorithm by proposing two novel
algorithms, the augmented DQN (ADQN) algorithm and the stochastic augmented DQN (SADQN)
algorithm. Computational results indicate that ADQN and SADQN solve the problem much faster
than DQN, with better solution qualities. The ADQN and SADQN algorithms provide flexibility for
practitioners in real-world implementations.

However, challenges still remain in utilizing Li-ion bat-
teries in the residential sector. One of the main practical
challenges is that Li-ion batteries often require a battery
management system (Parfomak, 2012). This management
system is an electronic system with a specialized algorithm
that ensures the safety and efficiency of battery operations
(Barsukov and Qian, 2013). The strategies of battery man-
agement originate from health monitoring and prognostics
of machinery, but have developed sizable differences. Since
Li-ion batteries show electro-chemical behaviors, the
inaccessibility of the chemical reactions inside the batteries
causes inconvenience in acquiring battery data, often leaving
insufficient data to analyze. Also, monitoring Li-ion batteries
results in different types of data from machinery observa-
tion, i.e., value-type instead of wave-form data. In addition,
Li-ion batteries operate on dynamic profiles that heavily
depend on the demand behavior. Thus, the available tech-
nologies and algorithms for diagnostics and prognostics of
machinery need to be updated before they can be applied to
Li-ion batteries (Zhang and Lee, 2011).
Battery management strategies have been intensively
studied in the context of integrating PV systems with battery
storage units. Specifically, studies have been performed to
estimate the state-of-charge voltage, capacity, and remain-
ing-useful-life in the battery using various approaches, such
as linear/nonlinear programming (Keerthisinghe et al., 2014;
Ratnam et al., 2015a; Ranaweera et al., 2017; Jiang et al.,
2021), dynamic programming (Keerthisinghe et al., 2016;
Ranaweera and Midtgård, 2016; Jeddi et al., 2017), heuristic
algorithm (Fuselli et al., 2013; Pena-Bello et al., 2017) or
simulation (Schibuola et al., 2017). A majority of the studies
present results of battery scheduling and management strat-
egies within a short horizon of 24 hours, with several
exceptions that project system performances for weeks or
even years (Ratnam et al., 2015b; Hassan et al., 2017; Olaszi
and Ladanyi, 2017; Watari et al., 2021). Considering that the
approximated lifespan of the Li-ion battery is 20 years
(Dufo-Lopez et al., 2021), long-term decision making is
essential in assessing the cost-effectiveness of the Li-ion bat-
tery and the integrated PV–battery system for residen-
tial users.
One of the major disadvantages in long-term battery
management strategy analysis is increasing model complex-
ity such that solving the model often becomes computation-
ally expensive or intractable. Since the battery system is
charged with PV-generated electricity, modeling battery
behavior must consider the uncertainties in PV power gen-
eration. Favored by many, optimization models, such as sto-
chastic programming, usually adopt a scenario-based
approach to model uncertainties in power generation, result-
ing in a multi-stage model and a tree structure of scenarios
that expands exponentially with the length of the horizon.
As a consequence, many current studies have considered
uncertainties as fixed parameters at different time-steps
(Hassan et al., 2017; Mulleriyawage and Shen, 2020; Watari
et al., 2021). These models need to be re-optimized if the
uncertainty parameters, such as the PV-generated power,
were to change.
In this article, we aim to develop a battery management
strategy that dynamically adapts to the changing environ-
ment. In order to model the operations of the integrated
PV–battery system, we develop a Markov Decision Process
(MDP) model. MDPs have been widely adopted in the lit-
erature to model system degradation and to derive optimal
policies in a wide range of applications, including the
PV–battery system (Keerthisinghe et al., 2014; Raju et al.,
2014; Barnes et al., 2015; Raju et al., 2015; Mbuwir et al.,
2017). Different from past studies, where battery degradation
is not thoroughly studied under uncertain environments,
our proposed MDP model optimizes the battery manage-
ment policy for the PV–battery system and captures the sto-
chastic environment that impacts PV output and battery
degradation.
Since PV panels are only functional when there is sun-
light, we separate each day into two periods, the day-time
and the night-time. As our problem of interest involves bat-
tery management and due to the fact that frequently charg-
ing and discharging the battery expedite its degradation and
negatively impact its lifespan, we incorporate a well-estab-
lished physics-based model from the literature into the
MDP to model battery aging (Xu et al., 2016). We model
battery degradation in a dynamic programming fashion (Xu,
2021), producing battery management policies in longer
terms than the literature (Shi et al., 2018). In addition, we
focus our attention on PV–battery systems that only allow
for charging the battery during the day-time and discharging
it during the night-time. Hence, the day-time demand is dir-
ectly satisfied by either the PV-generated electricity or elec-
tricity purchased from the grid (Walker, 2018), and the
night-time demand is satisfied by either the battery or elec-
tricity purchased from the grid.

or keep it. If the MDP decides to keep the battery, it then

to be charged, while accounting for peak sunlight hours
(subject to weather uncertainties and household demand).

discharge to satisfy the household demand. If the reserved
power is insufficient to address the energy demand, extra
electricity is purchased from the grid. As such, the policy
space is very large, mainly due to the large number of sys-

Often, MDP models are difficult to implement on large-
scale problems, due to the curse of dimensionality (de Farias
and Van Roy, 2003), i.e., the scale of the problem becomes
too large for traditional methods to be used in the optimiza-
tion process. However, recent advances in Reinforcement
Learning (RL) have paved the way for finding (near) optimal
policies of large-scale MDP problems. In RL, the decision
maker learns about the optimal policy through a series of
unsupervised trial-and-error procedures, i.e., evaluating the
learned policy while interacting with the environment.
Especially, the integration of RL and Neural Networks
(NNs) has extended the capabilities of RL algorithms to a
higher level. Combining deep NNs with RL, i.e., Deep RL
(DRL) (Mnih et al., 2015), has resulted in numerous suc-
cessful implementations in a variety of fields (Levine et al.,
2016; Silver et al., 2016).
One of the most successful DRL algorithms is the Deep
Q-Network (DQN), which has achieved human–level control
in playing Atari games (Mnih et al., 2015). The DQN makes
improvements due to a reduction in the reliance on domain
knowledge through the implementation of stochastic gradi-
ent descent in automatic feature engineering and end-to-end
learning. In this study, we utilize the DQN to overcome the
curse of dimensionality and to obtain approximate optimal
policy for the MDP. Moreover, to decrease the solution time
further, we provide two extensions to the DQN by incorpo-
rating structural properties of the MDP.
Since accurate simulations of battery degradation require
a large amount of data to account for various factors, we
further adopt a physics-based Machine Learning (ML)
approach in this study. Physics-based ML is a growing and
promising area of research in artificial intelligence (Gumiere
et al., 2020; Vadyala et al., 2021). It combines the power of
ML algorithms, such as DRL, with physics-based models, so
that ML algorithms learn not only from a simulated envir-
onment, but also from models built on concrete physics
foundations (Willard et al., 2020). Specifically, we use DRL
algorithms to simulate the cost and benefit of battery man-
agement policies, and use a well-established physics model
in the literature to calculate battery degradation (Xu et al.,
2016). In this way, the DRL algorithm demands less data for
simulation, but can still accurately model battery
degradation.
In the literature, only a few studies have considered the
optimal operations of PV–battery systems in the long term
(Raju et al., 2014; Raju et al., 2015; Nyholm et al., 2016;
Hassan et al., 2017; Olaszi and Ladanyi, 2017), among
which even fewer modeled either environmental uncertain-
ties or battery degradation (Raju et al., 2014; Rau et al.,
2015), due to the complexity imposed on the model. We
summarize the current research progress and trends regard-
ing battery management policies for PV systems in
Appendix A. Our study differs from the current literature in
significant ways, as it takes into account both uncertainties
in PV–battery operations as well as the battery degradation.
Further, different from other works in the literature, our
study establishes analytical properties of the model, which
are leveraged to improve the performance of solution algo-
rithms. This study is also among the first that adopts state-
of-the-art DRL methods to find operational policies for
PV–battery systems, contributing to the development of
smart systems with artificial intelligence technologies.
The main contributions of this study are as follows. First,
we develop an MDP model to optimally control battery util-
ization in storage-battery-integrated PV systems for residen-
tial users. Second, we optimize the financial cost of the
integrated PV–battery system during a 2-month horizon,
providing intuitive results for real-world implementations.
Third, we specifically focus on the longevity of the battery,
offering superior battery management policies compared
with a commonly used method in practice. Last, but not
least, we analytically establish mathematical properties of the
MDP model to design novel and efficient algorithms to opti-
mize battery management policies. The proposed algorithms
significantly differ from established algorithms in the litera-
ture and feature the combination of operations research and
artificial intelligence techniques, where mathematical proper-
ties unique to our problem are incorporated into backward
induction and DRL algorithms to improve performance.
This article is structured as follows. In Section 2, the key
notation is defined and the MDP model is formulated. In
Section 3, the MDP model is further analyzed to establish
structural properties. In Section 4, results of numerical stud-
ies are presented, including visualization of the optimal poli-
cies and comparisons with benchmarks. In Section 5,
solution algorithms are improved based on the structural
properties that are either proved mathematically or observed
in the results. Finally, in Section 6, we draw conclusions and
provide insights.

higher level. Combining deep NNs with RL, i.e., Deep RL
(DRL) (Mnih et al., 2015), has resulted in numerous suc-
cessful implementations in a variety of fields (Levine et al.,
2016; Silver et al., 2016).
One of the most successful DRL algorithms is the Deep
Q-Network (DQN), which has achieved human–level control
in playing Atari games (Mnih et al., 2015). The DQN makes
improvements due to a reduction in the reliance on domain
knowledge through the implementation of stochastic gradi-
ent descent in automatic feature engineering and end-to-end
learning. In this study, we utilize the DQN to overcome the
curse of dimensionality and to obtain approximate optimal
policy for the MDP. Moreover, to decrease the solution time
further, we provide two extensions to the DQN by incorpo-
rating structural properties of the MDP.
Since accurate simulations of battery degradation require
a large amount of data to account for various factors, we
further adopt a physics-based Machine Learning (ML)
approach in this study. Physics-based ML is a growing and
promising area of research in artificial intelligence (Gumiere
et al., 2020; Vadyala et al., 2021). It combines the power of
ML algorithms, such as DRL, with physics-based models, so
that ML algorithms learn not only from a simulated envir-
onment, but also from models built on concrete physics
foundations (Willard et al., 2020). Specifically, we use DRL
algorithms to simulate the cost and benefit of battery man-
agement policies, and use a well-established physics model
in the literature to calculate battery degradation (Xu et al.,
2016). In this way, the DRL algorithm demands less data for
simulation, but can still accurately model battery
degradation.
In the literature, only a few studies have considered the
optimal operations of PV–battery systems in the long term
(Raju et al., 2014; Raju et al., 2015; Nyholm et al., 2016;
Hassan et al., 2017; Olaszi and Ladanyi, 2017), among
which even fewer modeled either environmental uncertain-
ties or battery degradation (Raju et al., 2014; Rau et al.,
2015), due to the complexity imposed on the model. We
summarize the current research progress and trends regard-
ing battery management policies for PV systems in
Appendix A. Our study differs from the current literature in
significant ways, as it takes into account both uncertainties
in PV–battery operations as well as the battery degradation.
Further, different from other works in the literature, our
study establishes analytical properties of the model, which
are leveraged to improve the performance of solution algo-
rithms. This study is also among the first that adopts state-
of-the-art DRL methods to find operational policies for
PV–battery systems, contributing to the development of
smart systems with artificial intelligence technologies.
The main contributions of this study are as follows. First,
we develop an MDP model to optimally control battery util-
ization in storage-battery-integrated PV systems for residen-
tial users. Second, we optimize the financial cost of the
integrated PV–battery system during a 2-month horizon,
providing intuitive results for real-world implementations.
Third, we specifically focus on the longevity of the battery,
offering superior battery management policies compared
with a commonly used method in practice. Last, but not
least, we analytically establish mathematical properties of the
MDP model to design novel and efficient algorithms to opti-
mize battery management policies. The proposed algorithms
significantly differ from established algorithms in the litera-
ture and feature the combination of operations research and
artificial intelligence techniques, where mathematical proper-
ties unique to our problem are incorporated into backward
induction and DRL algorithms to improve performance.
This article is structured as follows. In Section 2, the key
notation is defined and the MDP model is formulated. In
Section 3, the MDP model is further analyzed to establish
structural properties. In Section 4, results of numerical stud-
ies are presented, including visualization of the optimal poli-
cies and comparisons with benchmarks. In Section 5,
solution algorithms are improved based on the structural
properties that are either proved mathematically or observed
in the results. Finally, in Section 6, we draw conclusions and
provide insights.

spans.content: 5.2. Algorithm comparison
In this section, we evaluate the solution quality and compu-
tational time of the developed algorithms, namely, modified
BI, ADQN and SADQN. We compare the results between
modified BI, DQN, ADQN and SADQN, using modified BI
as the benchmark, as it guarantees the optimality of the sol-
utions. Note that we do not include the results of regular BI
since preliminary results show that regular BI always per-
forms worse than modified BI. As discussed, since heuristic
search algorithms can also be used to optimize MDP prob-
lems, in Appendix F, we provide experiment results to show
that the DQN algorithm is more suitable to solve our MDP
problem than heuristic search algorithms.
We generate 12 cases using different scenarios of peak
sunlight hours with various horizons
(T_{m a x})
, as shown in
Table 3. To fully incorporate stochastic peak sunlight hours
in these cases, we consider three scenarios estimated from
real-world weather data, where in each scenario, we run the
model using four different horizons
(T_{m a x})
, representing
short-term (30 days), medium-term (60 and 120 days) and
long-term (365 days) operations. Specifically, in the first
scenario (Cases 1–4), we include two weather conditions:
Clear or cloudy, defined by the National Center for
Environmental Information
(National Center
for
Environmental Information, 2019). Clear and cloudy days
are estimated to have 6 and 4 hours of peak sunlight hours
(Sengupta et al., 2018). The probabilities of clear and cloudy
days follow the discrete distribution of [0.27, 0.73] (National
Center for Environmental Information, 2019). In the second
scenario (Cases 5–8), three weather conditions are consid-
ered: Clear, partly cloudy, and cloudy, estimated to have 6, 4
and 2 hours of peak sunlight hours (Sengupta et al., 2018),
with probabilities [0.27, 0.29, 0.44] (National Center for
Environmental Information, 2019). In the third scenario
(Cases 9–12), we expand the second scenario with further
granularity. We consider peak sunlight hours of 6, 5, 4, 3, 2,
Note that although this scenario may not be completely
drawn from historical data, it generally follows the observed
patterns and is considered as it provides a sufficiently
dynamic environment to test algorithm performances. Other
model parameters not specified here are consistent with
Section 4.

6. Conclusion and future work
In this study, we develop an integrated charge/discharge
scheme for Li-ion batteries to maximize their total expected
benefit. Specifically, we develop an MDP model to optimally
decide the charge/discharge levels of the PV–battery system
to satisfy the electricity demand for residential users under a
stochastic environment. In addition, we study the mathem-
atical properties of the MDP model, and establish the exist-
ence of a threshold-type optimal policy. This property, along
with observations made about the policy, is further leveraged
to devise new algorithms. Specifically, due to the extremely
slow rate of degradation in batteries, the state space of the
MDP is excessively large. Thus, we propose novel solution
algorithms, namely, modified BI, ADQN and SADQN, to
solve the problem efficiently. The proposed algorithms heav-
ily modify established algorithms in the literature, i.e., BI
and DQN, by leveraging the established structural properties
and observations. Numerical studies show that the MDP
model produces an intuitive optimal policy, which outper-
forms a commonly used battery replacement policy in prac-
tice. The results also indicate that the proposed ADQN and
SADQN algorithms produce faster and better solutions than
established benchmark algorithms from the literature.

There are limitations to this study that call for further
research. First, the electricity demand of the residential user
is simplified, such that only the demand during the night-
time are taken into consideration. The MDP model can be
extended with more detailed modeling regarding dynamic
demand structures in both day-time and night-time that
highlight peak usage hours. Second, we have only modeled
the peak sunlight hours using a probability distribution, but
more uncertainties can be incorporated, such as weather
conditions and seasonality, which impose bigger challenges
on efficient solution algorithms. Third, the maximum avail-
able battery capacity is assumed to be observable by the
model. In practice, noisiness in battery capacity measure-
ment presents opportunities to use partially observable MDP
to model the battery state of health. Finally, this study
employs household data averaged across an entire city, lack-
ing the case study using the data collected from individual
real-world households. It would be interesting to study the
performance of the MDP model implemented on real-world
households using their individual electricity demand data,
including more realistic electricity loads such as charging
electric vehicles.
